input.text: Your total is coming out too small in every case, and in the single-number case it's zero. Think about which list positions your loop actually visits when it adds numbers together — does it include the very first number in the line?

content.text: The diagnosis: your summing loop skips the first number in the list, so the first value never gets added to the total. That explains why each result is missing exactly the first input number (and why a single number sums to zero).

input.text: Look at the range in your for-loop on the line where you add to total. Its starting value controls which index is visited first — right now the first index in the list is never visited. Ask yourself which index the list actually begins at.

content.text: Your loop's starting index is one too high, so the first element is skipped. Check the range start against how Python lists are indexed.

input.text: Python lists are zero-indexed, so the first item is at index 0, not index 1. Your loop begins at 1 and therefore never adds the item at index 0. To sum every element, the loop must start at the first index, 0, and continue while the index is less than the list length. That single-number case sums to zero because the only item sits at index 0, which your loop skips entirely.

content.text: Your loop starts at index 1 instead of index 0, so the first element is always skipped. Starting the loop at 0 will include every number in the sum.
